We evaluate our method across multiple datasets, encoders, and LVLMs. ViSAR retrieves compact, query-adapted page sets that reduce end-to-end RAG latency by up to 58.9\%, with no statistically significant accuracy loss and significant gains in several settings, compared with fixed top-$k$ and adaptive retrieval heuristics. Furthermore, we show that the similarity matrix structure correlates with answer accuracy, suggesting future directions for retrieval quality-aware document understanding.

Information Retrieval.title: SearchJev: A Calibrated System-1 Model for Search Agents
Information Retrieval.summary: Search agents repeatedly make short decisions about relevance, evidence sufficiency, and search actions. Using generative language models for these decisions introduces latency and unreliable confidence. We present SearchJev, a calibrated System-1 model that separates search decisions from System-2 reasoning and generation. Given a search state and a decision schema, SearchJev scores legal options without autoregressive output generation. We propose Soft-Label Learning for Calibrated Decisions (SLCD) to learn decision probabilities from uncertain supervision and improve the reliability of decision confidence. In a dual-system search agent, SearchJev handles short decisions and delegates uncertain judgments to System 2, which retains planning, query generation, and answer composition. We also introduce SearchDecision-Bench, a benchmark unifying six types of search decisions for training and evaluation. On SearchDecision-Bench, SearchJev improves decision quality over same-size Qwen3.5 autoregressive models, achieves 5.2-5.3 times faster decisions, and reduces average expected calibration error by 41-74%. On BrowseComp-Plus, the dual-system agents achieve a 3.7-4.7 times speedup in active search time while improving answer accuracy from 45% to up to 54%.

Information Retrieval.title: EE-Motion: An EEG-based Web Architecture for Live Affective Music Recommendation
Information Retrieval.summary: Music listening is intrinsically tied to emotion, which drifts continuously within a single session. Although modern browsers interface with wearable brain-computer interfaces, recommendation systems remain structured around discrete logs and lack the infrastructure to integrate continuous physiological signals. Furthermore, existing affect-aware models rely on static user profiles and offline training, failing to serve anonymous newcomers without model retraining. We present a web platform that resolves both challenges. Pairing with a consumer electroencephalogram (EEG) headband over Web Bluetooth, the system captures live EEG, mapping frontal alpha asymmetry and arousal index to normalized valence-arousal proxy coordinates on Russell's circumplex plane. Driven by these coordinates, an affective adapter unifies structurally diverse recommendation backbones under a shared live scoring mechanism. By parameterizing anonymous visitors through a few favorite tracks, the module recommends tracks conditioned on live proxy coordinates. This demonstrates that real-time EEG-derived control signals can steer recommendations without persistent user tables or model retraining.

Information Retrieval.title: Adaptive-Elbow Graph Traversal for Schema Retrieval in Text-to-SQL
Information Retrieval.summary: LLM-based natural-language interfaces to relational databases are gated by a schema-retrieval step: the generator can only be as good as the slice of schema it is shown. On a database with hundreds of tables, that slice must be selected and the selection is two-sided---omit a needed table and the query becomes unrecoverable, include too many and the irrelevant ones act as noise that degrades the model's output. When an agentic retriever that lets the model inspect the schema can be too costly or too slow, the fallback is an embedder that ranks tables by cosine similarity and keeps a top-k. This fallback has two weaknesses: a fixed budget is suboptimal question by question, and embedding similarity overlooks foreign-key-linked tables that are necessary for joins. We present Adaptive-Elbow Graph Traversal (AEGT, ElbowHop for short), a property-graph table retriever that addresses both: an adaptive elbow cutoff replaces the fixed budget with a per-question one under a single aggressiveness parameter, and bidirectional foreign-key traversal deterministically recovers the bridge tables embedding similarity misses. We evaluate the retriever on 3 corpora of increasing candidate-pool size (BIRD Mini-Dev queried per database, 3--13 tables; its eleven schemas merged, 74; and a merged Spider-train graph, 546) and isolate the two mechanisms under a per-question budget-matched protocol. Across these settings the adaptive elbow emerges as the dominant mechanism---at matched recall it roughly doubles precision over a fixed budget on the larger pools, the margin widening as the pool grows---while the foreign-key traversal pays off on the join-critical bridge tables dense retrieval cannot reach, in the single-hop tight-budget case. We characterize the method as a low-cost, recall-robust first stage for schema retrieval on which a downstream selection or generation step can build.
Information Retrieval.comment: Presented at the 5th Italian Conference on Big Data and Data Science (ITADATA 2026). To appear in CEUR Workshop Proceedings

Information Retrieval.title: Living Context Graphs: Continual Semantic Learning for Enterprise Data Reasoning
Information Retrieval.summary: Enterprise AI can now perform analytics, reporting, and data-driven workflows, yet the data foundations it relies on remain hard to operationalize: business meaning, relationships, metric definitions, and reporting conventions are absent from database schemas and scattered across undocumented systems and tribal knowledge. We introduce the Living Context Graph (LCG), a continually learned context layer that makes existing enterprise data operational for AI without requiring a copy or transformation of the underlying warehouse. LCG bootstraps base semantics and relationships from the data itself, builds a concept graph that indexes business context as queries are served, writes durable semantic learnings from verified outcomes, and withdraws or re-earns context when later outcomes contradict prior routes. We evaluate LCG through text-to-SQL, a core data-reasoning task, on a transfer-aware split of three BIRD databases comprising 499 questions: 353 form the learning history and 146 are held out and never used to update the context layer. Bootstrapping alone improves overall accuracy by +4.6 percentage points. Learning only from the history raises accuracy on the untouched held-out transfer set by +22.6 points (95% CI [+14.4, +30.8]), exceeding five-shot retrieval from the same history by +12.3 points. Incremental learning reaches the one-shot endpoint within observed evaluation noise on every database. Ablating the graph changes held-out accuracy by at most one question per database but increases per-query cost 2.3-3.3x and median latency 1.8-3.4x: continually learned semantics drive accuracy, while the graph makes that context efficient to serve.
Information Retrieval.comment: 22 pages, 5 figures. Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Continual Learning in the Era of Foundation Models and Embodied Agents. Data splits and annotations: https://github.com/varunagrawal2002/Living-Context-Graph

Information Retrieval.title: Hi-Q: Hierarchical Evidence-guided Query Refinement for Multi-Hop Question Answering
Information Retrieval.summary: A central bottleneck in multi-hop Question Answering (QA) is that the granularity at which a question is expressed often differs from the granularity at which corpus evidence is retrievable. Existing methods address this mismatch by imposing fixed graph structures over the corpus, by iteratively reformulating the query, or by executing a generated program over it, but these strategies do not explicitly decide when a query unit is already supported by evidence and when it should be refined. We formulate this bottleneck as retrievable granularity discovery and introduce Hi-Q, an evidence-conditioned framework for hierarchical query refinement. At each query node, a resolution operator tests whether retrieved evidence supports the current query unit; resolved nodes terminate, while unresolved nodes are expanded by a dependency-preserving binary operator and checked by a semantic coverage verifier. Hi-Q therefore grows a query tree whose topology is determined by corpus support signals rather than by a fixed decomposition template or a pre-built graph. We evaluate Hi-Q on three multi-hop QA benchmarks, primarily under full-corpus retrieval, where dependent evidence must be located among open-domain distractors rather than within a small annotated pool. In this setting Hi-Q reaches 52.3 EM and 64.0 F1 averaged over the three benchmarks, ahead of the iterative retrieval baseline IRCoT by 15.1 EM / 18.2 F1 on that same average, and ahead of the graph-based RAG baseline PropRAG by 11.5 EM / 12.0 F1 on MuSiQue-full, without corpus-wide graph construction. In the restricted supporting/distractor setting used by prior work, Hi-Q likewise attains the best accuracy, with 57.9 EM and 69.3 F1 on average, ahead of PropRAG by 5.6 EM / 3.9 F1 and IRCoT by 13.7 EM / 15.8 F1. The project page is available at https://hi-q-project.github.io/.
Information Retrieval.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 28 pages, 11 figures. Project page: https://hi-q-project.github.io/

Information Retrieval.title: Evidence Diet: When Graph Evidence Helps LLMs Rank Competing Candidates
Information Retrieval.summary: When several candidates have graph support, does it matter which candidate receives which supporter and path counts? We study how LLM rankers use collaborative evidence on Amazon Books and MovieTV. Swapping user-level evidence degrades ranking, while matched item substitutions have little effect. On fixed clean-trained checkpoints, unrelated catalog text lowers Hit@1 from 44.77% to 38.70%, with 99.9% of rankings still valid. Across all three paired seeds, the NDCG@5 difference between count and path prompts was larger after count training than after path training. Degree matching preserves target paths while giving more rivals support. Across the full degree-matched development pools, adding candidate-level graph records to history improves NDCG@5 by 2.28 points on Books and 2.54 on MovieTV. When the target and a rival both have support, path- and count-trained rankers benefit from retaining counts. On these development queries, adding counts numerically to history scores outperforms presenting them as text. For count-trained rankers, exchanging intact count pairs among supported candidates preserves support and token length, yet lowers NDCG@5 by 4.06 points on 141 Books queries and 3.26 on 104 MovieTV queries. A frozen evaluation on 274 previously unused Books users with supported targets and rivals confirms the attribution effect: correct assignment improves pairwise accuracy by 6.07 percentage points (95% CI [4.18, 8.00]).

Information Retrieval.title: UniGraph: A Unified Graph-based Index for Dynamic Hybrid Dense-Sparse Vector Retrieval
Information Retrieval.summary: Hybrid dense-sparse vector retrieval combines semantic signals from dense representations with lexical signals from sparse representations, typically ranking items by a query-dependent weighted sum of dense and sparse vector distances. Existing systems commonly search separate dense and sparse vector indexes and rerank the union of their candidates, incurring two retrieval passes and potentially discarding items that rank highly only after the semantic and lexical signals are combined. Constructing a graph-based index directly under a hybrid distance can mitigate this premature candidate loss. However, because varying the hybrid weight alters the underlying neighborhood relationships, a single static graph built at a fixed weight cannot accommodate dynamic query-specific weights. Therefore, we propose a Unified Hybrid Graph (UniGraph), which merges neighbor sets computed at multiple hybrid weights into a single bounded-degree graph index, enabling hybrid vector retrieval with different query-specific weights without index reconstruction. We further develop an adaptive weight-guided search framework that chooses between sparse- and dense-guided entry points according to the query weight, together with a dense-first hybrid distance pruning strategy that avoids unnecessary exact sparse distance computations. Extensive experiments show that UniGraph provides a favorable Recall-QPS trade-off across different query weights. In the mixed-weight setting, UniGraph delivers 27.6%~52.3% higher QPS than the fastest baseline on each dataset at Recall@100 greater than or equal to 0.95. UniGraph has been deployed at scale in Ant Group's production environment, where hybrid retrieval with query-dependent weights is in strong demand.

Information Retrieval.title: CARE: Contrastive-Anchored Residual Encoding with Listwise Reconstruction for Retrieval-Oriented Semantic IDs
Information Retrieval.summary: Generative retrieval replaces nearest-neighbor search with the generation of a document's semantic ID (SID), so the SID tokenizer bounds what the retriever can recall. Common SID constructions (residual k-means, RQ-VAE, finite scalar quantization, capacity balancing) optimize criteria defined on document embeddings alone and do not control whether a query can still find its relevant documents after quantization. We propose two retrieval-oriented SID tokenizers. CARE-SID (Contrastive-Anchored Residual Encoding for Semantic IDs) quantizes in a retrieval-aligned space: a zero-initialized residual alignment network is trained with a query-document contrastive loss before quantization, an anchor loss and a reconstruction target fixed to the original embedding prevent drift and collapse, and reference-vector rating residual quantization assigns the codes. CARE-LR (CARE with Listwise Reconstruction) then distills, for each training query, the similarity distribution that the original embeddings induce over a candidate list into the SID reconstructions, through a function-preserving layer-resolved head. Both keep a document-only encoding interface. We judge SIDs without training a generator, by row-budget recall in a bucketing view (the partition) and a reconstruction view (the SID with its reconstruction). In offline evaluation on industrial video search data, both tokenizers achieve higher reconstruction-view recall than residual k-means, and CARE-LR improves further on CARE-SID, mainly through the listwise distillation. A comparison of two document embeddings shows that contrastive alignment helps most when the embedding has not been trained on search data, and that the embedding affects SID recall far more than the quantizer. CARE-SID is deployed in the generative retrieval stage of an industrial video search system.

Information Retrieval.title: When the Bill Falls: Reusing the Old Index Defers,Never Avoids, Re-encoding in Complete Embedding-Model Migration
Information Retrieval.summary: Upgrading the embedding model behind a vector index requires re-encoding the corpus. Recent work reuses the old index through adapters or window re-ranking. Across sixteen model pairs on passage and code corpora, plus eleven on Natural Questions (NQ), we find three results. First, reuse never avoids re-encoding: if migration must complete, every strategy eventually encodes every document; reuse only changes when that work is paid and the quality served meanwhile. Second, adapters should be compared with the old model, not only the new one. Of five adapter variants, only same-family LLM bridges beat the old model, and only by a negligible margin. Third, window re-ranking cost can be priced from the old index alone; pre-registered replays on all 8,841,823 passages confirmed the prediction on all three tested pairs. Workload skew also matters: across 36 further pre-registered Zipf replays, the planned family matched on 32. These findings yield three pre-migration rules: whether reuse is worthwhile, which strategy to use, and how deep a window to take. The depth rule priced every window that reached target quality to within 4 parts in 10^5 of the corpus. On NQ, a pre-committed plan selected the family on 10 of 11 pairs and priced every window exactly. Quality inputs transferred less reliably across corpus scale, so the model gap and window quality loss must be measured on the serving index.

Information Retrieval.title: UniFormer: Efficient and Unified Model-Centric Scaling for Industrial Recommendation
Information Retrieval.summary: Recently, substantial progress has been made in industrial recommendation through component-centric model scaling, where individual components such as behavior modeling, feature interaction, or task modeling are independently scaled to improve model capacity. Although recent methods such as HyFormer and OneTrans further explore cross-module co-scaling by jointly modeling behavior and interaction, their designs are still confined to the feature space and lack a unified model-centric scaling framework over the overall modeling space. In this paper, we propose UniFormer, an efficient and unified model-centric scaling framework for industrial recommender systems. To improve efficiency, UniFormer decomposes the overall modeling space into feature and task spaces, which are modeled by stacked Feature-space Interaction Modules and Task-space Interaction Modules, respectively. Moreover, UniFormer introduces semantic-based tokenization scheme to enable user-item decoupling, thereby achieving request-level inference acceleration. To prevent preference collapse, UniFormer employs multi-sequence cross-attention to separately capture heterogeneous behavior patterns, followed by the self-attention to enhance interaction modeling. Besides, dedicated multi-view FFNs are introduced to support flexible and scalable parameter scaling across different modeling components. Extensive online A/B testing in two production scenarios, Kuaishou and Kuaishou Lite, shows that UniFormer consistently improves user engagement and interaction metrics, achieving gains of +0.101%/+0.260% in App Stay Time and +0.729%/+1.113% in Watch Time, respectively.

Information Retrieval.title: CogRec: Structure-Cognitive Fast-and-Slow Reasoning for Generative Recommendation
Information Retrieval.summary: Generative recommendation reformulates next-item prediction as identifier sequence generation, yet existing methods mainly treat the generated identifiers as target sequences to be memorized, leaving their hierarchical and relational structure underused for explicit reasoning. We propose CogRec, a structure-cognitive fast-and-slow reasoning framework that grounds intermediate reasoning in the same SID topology used for target generation. CogRec augments the vertical SID hierarchy with intra-layer semantic graphs and introduces SID Routing to represent recommendation reasoning through layer-wise Match, LateralJump, and Explore operations. These operations provide a structural interpretation of fast localization and slow navigation. A supervised multi-stage pipeline aligns newly introduced SID tokens, establishes direct generation, and trains natural-language and SID Routing branches from a shared checkpoint. Experiments on three Amazon Reviews 2014 categories show dataset-dependent effects of SID Routing. Routing improves Hit@10 and NDCG@10 over its direct-generation counterpart on Beauty and Sports, while reducing both metrics on Toys. These results characterize the benefits and dataset-dependent behavior of SID-grounded intermediate reasoning for generative recommendation. Code is available at https://github.com/caskcsg/CogRec.

Information Retrieval.title: GateSID: One Gate to Balance Semantic and Collaborative Signals across the Item Lifecycle
Information Retrieval.summary: In recommender systems, collaborative signals work well for popular items but are nearly absent for cold-start ones. Semantic content helps new items, yet over-reliance on it blurs the behavioral distinctions of popular items. Existing Semantic ID (SID) based methods handle this trade-off only partially, because their fusion of the two signals is rigid and item-agnostic. We present GateSID, a ranking framework that takes SID from an upstream tokenizer and adapts how each SID is used to the item's maturity through a single shared gate. The gate drives three mechanisms. Gating-Fused Shared Attention (GFSA) fuses the attention distributions of the two modalities rather than their representations. Gate-Regulated Contrastive Alignment (GRCA) strengthens semantic-behavioral alignment for items with weak collaborative evidence and relaxes it when collaborative structure is reliable. Gate-Regulated Semantic Resolution (GRSR) uses coarse shared SID prefixes for items with weak behavioral evidence and opens deeper SID levels when the gate indicates more reliable collaborative evidence. On a large-scale industrial dataset, GateSID leads the strongest SID-enhanced baseline by +0.27% CTR AUC and +0.36% CTCVR GAUC, with gains balanced across item groups rather than trading cold-start for popular-item performance; on the public Taobao-MM benchmark, it also leads overall and gives the strongest new-item results under both DIN and RankMixer backbones. In a one-month online A/B test, GMV improves by 2.6%, CTR by 1.1%, and Order by 1.6%, at a cost of less than 5 ms of additional latency. We also provide a systematic analysis of SID design choices, covering embedding type, codebook configuration, and fusion strategy.

Information Retrieval.title: Unified Ranking Across Retrieval Channels: A Large-Scale E-Commerce Approach
Information Retrieval.summary: Large-scale e-commerce search and recommendation systems rely on multiple specialized retrieval channels to surface diverse products, each optimized for a distinct objective. A key challenge is merging candidates from these heterogeneous channels into a single ranked list under strict latency constraints while optimizing business KPIs such as user conversion. Static rank-fusion methods such as Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) and Weighted Interleaving use the same fusion behavior across queries, limiting their ability to adapt to context or model interactions among channel signals. We reformulate multi-channel fusion as a channel-aware learning-to-rank problem and propose a unified ranking model trained on a scalar, funnel-weighted graded-relevance label that combines clicks, add-to-carts, and purchases. The model incorporates channel-specific scores together with recent aggregate query-item behavior to capture near-term population demand. The evaluated channel set combines conventional relevance retrieval with query-conditioned, recommendation-oriented channels emphasizing newness, trending demand, regional relevance, and seasonality. A randomized online experiment shows a 2.85% increase in user conversion over the deployed weighted-interleaving control. The model achieves a p95 reranking-stage latency below 50 ms and has been deployed on Target.com.
Information Retrieval.comment: Accepted as a regular paper to the Industry & Government Program of the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Big Data (IEEE BigData 2026), Phoenix, AZ, December 14-17, 2026. 10 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables. v4: accepted version (revised title and text)

Information Retrieval.title: Why Steering Works: Toward a Unified View of Language Model Parameter Dynamics
Information Retrieval.summary: Methods for controlling large language models (LLMs), including local weight fine-tuning, LoRA-based adaptation, and activation-based interventions, are often studied in isolation, obscuring their connections and making comparison difficult. In this work, we present a unified view that frames these interventions as dynamic weight updates induced by a control signal, placing them within a single conceptual framework. Building on this view, we propose a unified preference-utility analysis that separates control effects into preference, defined as the tendency toward a target concept, and utility, defined as coherent and task-valid generation, and measures both on a shared log-odds scale using polarity-paired contrastive examples. Across methods, we observe a consistent trade-off between preference and utility: stronger control increases preference while predictably reducing utility. We further explain this behavior through an activation manifold perspective, in which control shifts representations along target-concept directions to enhance preference, while utility declines primarily when interventions push representations off the model's valid-generation manifold. Finally, we introduce a new steering approach SPLIT guided by this analysis that improves preference while better preserving utility. Code is available at https://github.com/zjunlp/EasyEdit/blob/main/examples/SPLIT.md.

Information Retrieval.title: Beyond Text: Text-Image Fusion for Scalable Two-Tower Retrieval
Information Retrieval.summary: E-commerce customers make purchase decisions by jointly considering product text and visual information, yet most industrial retrieval systems rely almost exclusively on textual signals. Deployed at scale on CPU-based nearest-neighbor infrastructure, these systems leave substantial visual evidence untapped. In this work, we study unified text-image fusion for two-tower retrieval models at a large-scale e-commerce platform, training on 20M query-item pairs. We demonstrate that domain-specific fine-tuning and modality-specific query alignment between user queries and both product text and image modalities are crucial for effective multimodal retrieval. Building on these insights, we propose a mixture-of-modality-experts fusion architecture with a bilinear interaction network to capture cross-modal complementary information. Our model achieves up to 4.86% improvement in nDCG@1 for desirability and 2.36% for relevance over a strong text-only baseline, while preserving the pre-computable item embedding design required for production deployment.

Information Retrieval.title: MAGE: Meta-path Adaptive Graph Evidence for Transferable Multimodal Graph Learning
Information Retrieval.summary: Multimodal graphs integrate textual and visual attributes with relational structures, providing a rich representation of complex real-world data. To enable the broad applicability and reuse of graph models, it is crucial for models trained on source graphs to generalize to unseen graph domains. However, this is challenging because cross-modal interactions among neighbors and the neighboring information needed for prediction can vary across target nodes and graph domains. This gives rise to two key challenges: adaptive cross-modal neighborhood fusion, which captures and integrates cross-modal interactions among neighbors to accommodate variations across nodes and domains; and target-specific evidence selection, which identifies the neighboring textual and visual information needed for each target node to support LLM-based prediction. In light of these challenges, we propose MAGE (Meta-path Adaptive Graph Evidence Prompting), a framework for transferable multimodal graph learning. MAGE represents textual and visual node views separately in a heterogeneous graph and introduces two complementary components. Meta-path Adaptive Multimodal Propagation (MAMP) adaptively aggregates neighborhood information along heterogeneous meta-paths and compresses it into graph-aware soft tokens. Evidence-Guided Instruction Tuning (EGIT) selects relevant neighboring evidence for each query and incorporates its graph-aware representations into instructions for a frozen multimodal LLM. Together, these components support transfer from multiple source graphs to unseen target graphs without target-domain parameter updates. Experiments with three source graphs and four unseen target graphs demonstrate strong cross-domain transfer performance on node classification and link prediction, without requiring parameter updates on the target domains.

Information Retrieval.title: IntentFlow: An Intent-Driven Real-Time Multimodal Search System with Image-Text Queries at Xiaohongshu
Information Retrieval.summary: Multimodal search with image-text queries helps users find notes in user-generated content (UGC) communities and serves as a key search tool for multimodal search agents. For such queries, query-note relevance depends on the user's retrieval intent and cannot be determined by visual or topical similarity alone. Simply reranking visual search results cannot fully address this challenge, as notes relevant to the user's intent may be missing from the initial candidate set. This motivates explicit intent modeling to align candidate retrieval and reranking under consistent relevance criteria. We present IntentFlow, an intent-driven real-time multimodal search system deployed at Xiaohongshu over an index on the order of ten billion entries. IntentFlow represents retrieval objectives with a hierarchical intent taxonomy and uses intent-specific relevance criteria to guide data construction, representation learning, and reranking. An offline agentic data workflow acquires candidates and verifies their relevance under these criteria to produce training supervision. The embedding model combines intent-aware contrastive learning, graded ranking, and distribution distillation, while a compact reranker assesses query-candidate evidence conditioned on predicted hierarchical intents. Evaluations demonstrate that IntentFlow delivers substantial gains in search engagement while supporting real-time search at industrial scale. In a user-level A/B test on the Xiaohongshu platform, IntentFlow outperforms the existing production system based on visual search followed by reranking, achieving relative gains of 28.17% in Top-4 query click-through rate, 18.96% in query click-through rate, and 12.56% in average time spent on search results pages per user. Production monitoring records an end-to-end P50 latency of 1.07 s.

Information Retrieval.title: Overview of the Plagiarism Detection Task at PAN 2026
Information Retrieval.summary: The generative plagiarism detection task at PAN 2026 aims at retrieving the original scientific sources for given automatically generated textual plagiarism. We created two novel datasets of synthetically generated plagiarism following the premise of a malicious actor trying to generate papers with minimal effort while evading detection of undisclosed re-use. We utilized four widely available LLMs: GPT-OSS 120B, Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen 3.5 27B FP8, and DeepSeek-R1 Distill Llama 8B. In this task overview paper, we outline the creation of this dataset and summarize and compare the results of all participants with three baselines. For this year's task, we received 26 submissions from six teams that significantly outperformed our baselines.
Information Retrieval.comment: Corrected version of the paper published in CEUR-WS Vol-4283: an error in the one-shot generation dataset was fixed and the one-shot results (Sec. 2.3, Table 3, Figs. 2, 3, 6) were updated; the sequential dataset and its results are unchanged. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23528623 (Version v3)

Information Retrieval.title: What Unlinked Aggregates Still Prove: Ranker Comparisons from Exact and Differentially Private Item Counts
Information Retrieval.summary: Privacy controls can prevent an evaluator from linking purchases to the recommendations users received, while a merchant can still release complete item-level purchase counts for the evaluation cohort. We ask when these counts identify which recommender performs better. The counts constrain who could have bought each item. We bound the performance difference over all assignments consistent with the counts. A reduced transportation network handles full catalogs and can certify attainable endpoints. If the interval excludes zero, it identifies the better recommender for that cohort. With differentially private counts, one confidence guarantee applies jointly to all comparisons from the same release. In two e-commerce cohorts of about 20,000 and 100,000 users, exact counts narrowed every interval compared with bounds that ignored the counts. Most decisions involved a recommender that favors popular items. For NDCG@10, which rewards ranking purchased items higher, each setting combined one of three personalized pairs with a pattern and rate of missing links. Exact counts settled 14 of 168 settings in the smaller cohort and none of 81 in the larger cohort. In the smaller cohort, exact counts broken down by user group settled two personalized pairs when 90% of users remained linked, at the cost of revealing more about individual purchases. Whole-cohort private releases with one count per item retained much of the narrowing but settled no personalized pair in either cohort. Grouping less popular items into bins let private counts settle one personalized pair in the smaller cohort.
Information Retrieval.comment: 10 pages, 4 figures. Accepted for publication in the Privacy and Security of Big Data special session at IEEE BigData 2026. Code available at https://github.com/AnthonyXu109/psbd26-artifact

Information Retrieval.title: Straight to the Product: What Online Retailers Miss When Shoppers Ask AI First
Information Retrieval.summary:
When people ask an AI assistant what to buy, what happens next at the store? We link the same people's assistant conversations to their later browsing at twenty large online retailers. People go to the product the assistant named: among shoppers who had not visited the store in the past week, visits to the named product within a day rise from 0.02 to 2.07 per 100 answers (+2.0 points [1.7, 2.4]), and on days with a product-page visit at the store, 44% show a product from their own answer, against 1.5% for a matched answer given to someone else. The result replicates in a separate five-month period. Few arrive through the assistant's link: 89% of visits carry no sign of it, and 54% follow a web search, the same share as their usual visits. When a search comes just before the first visit, it names the answer's product 28% of the time (1% in earlier weeks), as if the search box were an address bar. The chat names the product; the store logs a search. Once there, shoppers keep browsing.
  We propose product follow-through, the share of answers followed by a visit to the product they named, as a way to evaluate shopping assistants and agents by what people do next: it needs no referral data or provider logs and can be computed for each assistant.

Information Retrieval.title: Beyond Bitwidth: Deployment-Constrained Mixed-Precision Quantization for Multilingual LLM Inference on NVIDIA Blackwell
Information Retrieval.summary: Low-bit LLM quantization is useful only if a model preserves service-relevant accuracy, executes through supported GPU kernels, and meets measured memory and latency limits. We study Qwen3-8B on NVIDIA B200 with vLLM, including INT2/INT3, GPTQ, NVFP4, and mixed-precision configurations. We verify native packed execution and precision on all 144 fused linear modules and evaluate Korean, English, numerical, and reasoning quality under preregistered gates. Packed INT2 and INT3 execute, but all seven tested INT2 grids degenerate on generation. Isolated module-restoration effects are strongly non-additive; Korean and reasoning sensitivity rankings disagree, and a promising INT4/INT8 development candidate fails independent final evaluation. A configuration with 16-bit activations, 98 NVFP4 weight-only modules, 46 INT8 modules, and an INT8 output head passes all gates on the untouched FINAL-81 set (5,168 items): 5.917 GiB of weight-loading memory (limit 5.98), Korean teacher-correct retention 0.904 (gate 0.90), and TPOT ratio 0.939 relative to BF16. It improves paired accuracy over NVFP4 W4A4 by +1.4 percentage points (Bonferroni-adjusted interval [+0.2, +2.6]), compared with +3.4 points on the selection set. This comparison changes both activation precision and INT8 protection; exploratory analyses suggest that the activation change contributes substantially, but the isolated allocation effect is not established. Final checkpoints were not retained, and bitwise rebuild reproducibility remains unverified.

Information Retrieval.title: Complexity and precision in quantum associative retrieval
Information Retrieval.summary: We show that efficient and high-precision quantum associative retrieval is possible with an exponential complexity advantage with respect to the classical brute force approach and with a polynomial capacity advantage with respect to classical neural network implementations for any number of patterns scaling polynomially in the number of qubits. Both classical neural and quantum associative memories store the patterns in a Hamiltonian; in the classical case the dynamics is irreversible relaxation toward attractors, in the quantum case it is unitary transformations generating an effective thermal distribution, followed by a measurement.

Information Retrieval.title: Lightfoot: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Exact, Model-Free Document Deletion
Information Retrieval.summary: Graph-based retrieval-augmented generation (GraphRAG) improves multi-hop question answering, but deployed systems pay costs that research comparisons rarely measure: model calls at query time, building the graph, and removing documents correctly. We present Lightfoot, a GraphRAG system in which every entity, link, fact and synonym edge is a deterministic function of per-passage extractions that carry chunk-level provenance. Retrieval makes no language-model call, indexing makes one per passage, and deleting a document is a database transaction with no model calls: 14 seconds for 10% of an 11,402-passage corpus, after which the graph is identical to a fresh index of the surviving documents. On a corpus of near-duplicate names, HippoRAG 2's capped synonym lists leave 565 fewer edges than a rebuild, while Lightfoot remains exact. Under identical extraction, embedding and answer models on held-out questions of MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA and HotpotQA, Lightfoot is competitive with HippoRAG 2: with Holm-corrected paired tests it is better on MuSiQue at recall@5 and recall@10 (+4.8 and +5.5 points) and on 2WikiMultiHopQA at recall@10 (+3.4), and tied on HotpotQA, while HippoRAG 2 keeps a non-significant 3.0-point edge at 2WikiMultiHopQA recall@2. Seeding the walk from entities named in the question accounts for most of the 2WikiMultiHopQA gain. Answers tie on all three datasets, and the retrieval pattern holds with three larger embedders, up to Qwen3-Embedding-8B. The gain is not the reranker's: with the same cross-encoder, dense retrieval trails Lightfoot by 9.3 and 17.8 points recall@5 on the two multi-hop sets. Lightfoot also builds the cheapest index, 26-31% below HippoRAG 2; LightRAG needed 2,187 model calls and 3.7 hours for the same deletion, and fast-graphrag cannot delete.

Information Retrieval.title: Urban Representation Learning for Identifying Potential Disparities in Crime Reporting
Information Retrieval.summary: Open crime data support urban safety analysis but reflect reported incidents rather than the complete distribution of criminal activity, potentially introducing spatial distortions in downstream analysis. We propose a self-supervised urban representation learning framework for identifying unusual reporting patterns relative to representation-similar peers using only georeferenced crime records. The method constructs complementary hourly, weekly, and static reporting profiles, learns scale-specific representations under geographic self-supervision, and integrates them into a unified latent space. Neighbor Profile Divergence (NPD) is then used to quantify disagreement between each region's reporting profile and those of its retrieved peers. Experiments on more than 1.8 million crime records from Mexico City, aggregated into 1,058 H3 regions, show that the proposed representation achieves a mean Silhouette score of 0.4052, compared with 0.2863 for Hex2Vec. NPD rankings remain highly stable across neighborhood sizes, with Spearman correlations from 0.9720 to 0.9951, while most high-divergence candidates persist across configurations. The retrieved peers also extend substantially beyond immediate geographic neighborhoods, indicating that the learned representation captures structure beyond local spatial proximity. High-divergence regions exhibit spatially organized patterns and, in several cases, differences in incident volume relative to peer expectations. These results support NPD as an internal auditing and prioritization mechanism for identifying regions that warrant further investigation, rather than as direct evidence of underreporting.
Information Retrieval.comment: Accepted for publication in International Conference on Artificial Intelligence, Computer, Data Sciences, and Applications (ACDSA 2027)

Machine Learning.title: Latent Lattice Language Models
Machine Learning.summary: Language models typically increase per-token computation through deeper or looped layers and latent reasoning steps, while richer residual connections improve information flow across layers. We instead increase computational capacity: the number of active computational states a model maintains. We introduce the Lattice of Latents, a set of per-layer horizontal latent streams that run recurrently along time, alongside the vertical residual stream that flows through depth. Like hyper-connections, mHC, and attention or value residuals, the Lattice enhances the residual stream, but rather than adding or rerouting residual pathways through depth, it provides companion computational states that persist across tokens. Unlike hybrid Transformer-SSM architectures, whose recurrent states primarily serve as internal memory for sequence mixing, these latents directly condition the vertical stream's attention, KV-cache writes, MLP computation, and decoding. On Transformers trained on 20B FineWeb-Edu tokens, a 406M-parameter Lattice model lowers validation perplexity from 15.41 to 14.40 over a parameter-matched Transformer. These gains extend across architectural variants. The Lattice composes with prior residual-stream enhancements: with hyper-connections and input residuals, it lowers validation perplexity from 15.41 (base Transformer) and 14.22 (Transformer with the same enhancements) to 13.61. On Gated DeltaNet, Mamba-2, Triadic GDN, and GDN-Mamba-2 hybrids, it improves perplexity at every tested native state size, with Lattice-GDN and Lattice-Triadic-GDN variants outperforming pure baselines with 4x larger native states. These results identify persistent per-layer state as a complementary axis for scaling language-model computation.

Machine Learning.title: AI4BayesCode: From Natural Language Descriptions to Validated Modular Stateful Bayesian Samplers
Machine Learning.summary: Coding and computation remain major bottlenecks in Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) workflows, especially as modern sampling algorithms have become increasingly complex and existing probabilistic programming systems remain limited in model support, extensibility, and composability. We introduce AI4BayesCode, an extensible LLM-driven system that translates natural-language Bayesian model descriptions into runnable, validated MCMC samplers. To improve reliability, AI4BayesCode adopts a modular design that decomposes models into modular sampling blocks and maps each block to a built-in sampling component, reducing the need to implement complex sampling algorithms from scratch. Reliability is further improved through pre-generation validation of model specifications and post-generation validation of generated sampler code. AI4BayesCode also introduces a novel recursively stateful coding paradigm for MCMC, allowing modular sampling components, potentially developed by different contributors, to be composed coherently within larger MCMC procedures. We develop a benchmark suite to evaluate AI4BayesCode for sampler-generation. Experiments show that AI4BayesCode can implement a wide range of Bayesian models from natural-language descriptions alone. As an open-ended system, its capability can continue to expand with improvements in the underlying AI agent and the addition of new built-in blocks. The software is available at https://ai4bayescode.com/.

Machine Learning.title: Quantifying the added value of human forecaster discussions for tropical cyclone intensity prediction
Machine Learning.summary: The National Hurricane Center routinely releases Tropical Cyclone Discussions that offer insights into its tropical cyclone forecasts. This study examines the added value of these discussions for intensity forecasting beyond a set of numerical predictors. For 637 Atlantic and eastern North Pacific tropical cyclones from the 2002-2023 hurricane seasons, we analyze the discussion text and its combination with 13 hurricane environmental predictors from SHIPS and ERA5 10-meter wind fields, for forecasting intensity changes at lead times of 24 to 120 hours using three modeling methods. In one approach, an end-to-end deep learning framework for the text shows that the discussions alone offer comparable value for 24-hour intensity forecasts to the SHIPS predictors. Adding discussion information to the SHIPS predictors in an ensemble of five such models reduces the mean absolute error of 24-hour maximum sustained wind forecasts for 2022-2023 cyclones from 9.89 to 8.90 kt, with a confidence interval that excludes zero when whole storms are resampled. The ERA5 wind fields have a minor effect on mean absolute error in wind predictions, and model rankings differ across predicted variables, lead times and model types. We provide prediction intervals for these forecasts, whose coverage falls below the 90% target during rapid intensification. Analysis of the text shows that words related to intensity and intensity change (such as intensify, weaken, eyewall and category) are important for the model predictions. This retrospective study shows the added value of the forecasters' discussions and suggests that multi-modal learning can help understand the predictive contribution of expert human judgment. The reanalysis data differ from real-time analyses, and the discussions are issued at least three hours after the valid time of the other inputs, so these results should not be interpreted operationally.

Machine Learning.title: How VLMs Plan What's Next
Machine Learning.summary: When a vision-language model describes an image, it names one object at a time and it rarely repeats itself, yet how the model plans this order is far from obvious. We characterize the mechanism a VLM uses to decide where to look before it looks. The mechanism has four main parts. First, binding heads match the relevant text tokens against the image and resolve them into pointers to the matched image region. Second, the same binding heads bind each written answer to the region it came from, and the model turns it into a progress signal: a cursor, the position in the image up to which the list has been written. Third, a select step chooses the nearest unwritten region after the cursor, or stops. Finally, gaze heads execute the chosen pointer and return a concept of what is drawn there, which language heads and the late MLPs turn into a word in the language of the question. We validate each part of this mechanism through causal patching in Qwen3-VL models on a synthetic visual retrieval task, and test our mechanisms against alternative hypotheses. We further show that the mechanism holds across input formats, natural photographs, and languages, and that its binding, relay, and gaze heads appear at every model size from 2B to 32B. This work allows us to investigate how a VLM turns a question and an image into a sequence of answers, layer by layer and token by token. More broadly, it opens a way to study how models plan over complex multi-step tasks with long rollouts. Our project is available at https://plan.baulab.info/

Machine Learning.title: Hyperlyve: Parallelized Enumeration and Exact Lyapunov Stability Certification for Deep ReLU Networks
Machine Learning.summary: We introduce Hyperlyve (Hyperplane Partitioned Lyapunov Verification and Enumeration), a framework for proving the asymptotic stability of nonlinear dynamical systems, including those with neural network controllers. Hyperlyve learns and formally certifies continuous piecewise-affine (CPA) neural Lyapunov functions within a counterexample-guided inductive synthesis (CEGIS) loop. Hyperlyve's key innovation is a parallel algorithm that enumerates the hyperplane arrangement formed by the ReLU activations of deep networks and certifies that Lyapunov conditions hold within each polyhedral region. We derive sound and complete regional tests to verify the asymptotic stability of the exact smooth dynamics (rather than a piecewise-linear approximation) within a compact domain of interest. Furthermore, we formally characterize the computational complexity of the CPA neural Lyapunov verification problem as co-NP-complete, filling a key gap in the literature. Empirical results demonstrate that Hyperlyve enumerates ReLU networks over 150-times faster than competing tools, which contributes to Hyperlyve proving the asymptotic stability of systems that are currently intractable for state-of-the-art verifiers.

Machine Learning.title: Mitigating Catastrophic Forgetting with Physics-Indexed Specialist Memory: the Evolutionary Neuroplastic Agent
Machine Learning.summary: Continual reinforcement learning requires adaptation to changing conditions while preserving performance under previously encountered dynamics. It was investigated whether specialists generated by evolutionary search can provide a reusable memory when combined with environment detection and failure-driven search. The Evolutionary Neuroplastic Agent (ENA) evolves small neural networks without gradients, archives selected policies by detected dynamic regime, and retrieves them through Bayesian policy reuse. The architecture was evaluated in non-stationary CartPole and HalfCheetah environments. In the 30-replicate CartPole ablation, the complete architecture achieved a mean success rate of 83.2% across the five test environments. Among variants that learned the harder CartPole environments, the complete architecture showed the most consistent retention. A selection ablation also showed that the retrieval rule affected performance. In the evaluated sequences, ENA adapted more slowly than PPO on CartPole and achieved lower returns than SAC on HalfCheetah. The evidence concerns the complete architecture and does not isolate gradient-free optimization as the cause of retention or establish superiority over other continual-learning methods.
Machine Learning.comment: 25 pages, 7 figures, 23 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/blasvicco/ena/tree/v1

Machine Learning.title: Optimal Autoregressive Chain-of-Thought Learning via Bagging
Machine Learning.summary: We study how to learn an autoregressive next-token generator $f\colonΣ^\star\toΣ$ from a class $\mathcal{F}$, given chain-of-thought (CoT) demonstrations of length $T$ generated by $f$. We present a simple algorithm based on bagging, which outputs a majority vote of generators that are trained to be CoT-consistent on bootstrap samples of the training data. For binary token sets, it achieves the optimal sample complexity of $O((d_{\mathrm{VC}}+\log(1/δ))/ε)$, independent of the CoT length $T$, where $d_{\mathrm{VC}}$ is the VC dimension of $\mathcal{F}$. For finite token sets $Σ$, the VC dimension is replaced by a multiclass analogue, the Graph dimension $d_{\mathrm{G}}$, and the sample complexity is optimal up to a $\log|Σ|$ factor. The number of generators in the majority-vote ensemble is $O(\log(T/δ))$, and we show that the ensemble can be distilled into a single generator in $\mathcal{F}$ at the expense of $n\log(nT)$ unlabeled prompts.

Machine Learning.title: SADL: On the Demand-Supply Geometry of Representation Collapse
Machine Learning.summary: In Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs), a well-constrained projector output does not by itself prevent representation collapse. We find that, from initialization, the encoder representation is dominated by a component shared by different inputs. A batch-normalized projector removes this component, so regularization after the projector cannot correct it, and the differences between representations shrink until they collapse. We propose SADL (Supply And Demand Loss), which keeps the original training objective and constrains the encoder directly when needed. SADL compares the representation differences that the projector output demands with the differences the encoder can retain and pass on to the projector, and adds a constraint on the encoder only when supply falls short of demand. It works with different Demand Regularizers and introduces no auxiliary networks, additional trainable parameters, or architectural changes. In single-task and jointly trained four-task LeWorldModel (LeWM) and INTACT experiments, SADL lowers the collapse rate over ten random seeds from 50% to 0%. After one epoch of training, encoder effective rank is 3.4-6.4 times that of the corresponding baseline without SADL, and latent prediction error falls to 1/20-1/303 of it. Without additional tuning, SADL stays robust as its loss weight spans orders of magnitude, and with several Demand Regularizers INTACT exceeds 95% mean search-free control success. On four image datasets, SADL also consistently improves accuracy and stability across random seeds. These results show that matching the representation differences a regularizer demands with the differences the encoder can supply leads to faster and more stable representation learning in control and image classification.

Machine Learning.title: Surrogate-Assisted Compact-Model Extraction for SKY130 CMOS at 77 K
Machine Learning.summary: Cryogenic circuit design requires compact transistor models that reproduce measured low-temperature behavior and run in standard circuit simulators. We fit BSIM4 parameters to measured I-V curves of SkyWater 130 nm (SKY130) transistors at 77 K using a neural surrogate of NGSpice. The surrogate maps compact-model parameters and device geometry to the complete set of output and transfer characteristics. Extraction is a bounded least-squares search: a bank of NGSpice simulations supplies initial candidates, finite differences of the surrogate supply the local Jacobian, and NGSpice re-simulates the resulting cards before selection. On 18 measured geometries, we compare a search over seven card parameters with a search over 43 parameters selected by NGSpice sensitivity. Relative to NGSpice re-simulations of the previously released cards, the two searches reduce the in-sample mean relative root-mean-square error (RRMS) by 17% and 26%, respectively. The 43-parameter search has the lower overall error, but the seven-parameter search has the lower mean on high-bias curves, and some individual curves have higher error than with the released cards under both searches.

Machine Learning.title: CertiSum: Bitwise-Identical MXFP4 Training Across Platforms and Parallelism Layouts
Machine Learning.summary: Training with MXFP4, a 4-bit microscaling format, is non-deterministic: identical inputs can produce different results across parallelism layouts and GPU vendors. These differences complicate debugging and training audits and can cause training and inference engines to disagree. We present CertiSum to make MXFP4 training bitwise invariant across runs, parallelism layouts, and GPU vendors. Its key insight is that native FP32 accumulation of MXFP4 products is often already exact for every summation order. CertiSum collects statistics during quantization to certify native matrix multiplication results, recomputes uncertified outputs exactly, and uses exact kernels directly where certification rarely succeeds. CertiSum keeps quantization blocks unchanged across layouts and merges partial sums without rounding, including in attention and weight-gradient computation. In 200-step Qwen3-8B-Base experiments, CertiSum preserves training states bit for bit across AMD MI350X and NVIDIA GB200 and across changes in data, tensor, and context parallelism on MI350X. Across three 8B--14B models on FineWeb-Edu using MI350X, it adds 11.8--60.5% to training-step latency relative to its non-exact MXFP4 counterpart at the larger evaluated input shapes, with speedups of up to $1.24\times$ over BF16 and $1.70\times$ over deterministic BF16.

Machine Learning.title: A Systematic Analysis of Out-of-Distribution Detection Under Representation and Training Paradigm Shifts
Machine Learning.summary: We present a systematic benchmark of out-of-distribution (OOD) detection confidence scoring functions (CSFs) through a representation-centric lens. Our study spans CNN and ViT backbones, multiple training paradigms, four image-classification source datasets (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SuperCIFAR-100, and TinyImageNet), and OOD datasets grouped into near, mid, and far regimes based on CLIP-derived semantic distances. To compare CSFs across these settings, we employ a rank-based pipeline of Friedman and Conover tests that identifies top cliques of statistically indistinguishable winners under threshold-free ranking metrics (AURC and AUGRC). The main empirical finding is that the family of CSFs that are competitive detectors correlates with characteristics of the learned representation. For both CNNs and ViTs, simple probabilistic scores dominate misclassification detection. On CNNs, margin-based scores are strongest in near-OOD regimes, while geometry-aware scores such as NNGuide, fDBD, and CTM become more competitive as shift severity increases. On fine-tuned ViTs, the top cliques are led mainly by reconstruction- and residual-based scores. To interpret these ranking shifts, we analyze the last-layer representation using Neural Collapse (NC) metrics. The resulting picture is consistent across architectures: prototype- and boundary-aware scores become stronger when the representation is more collapsed and better aligned with classifier weights, whereas weaker-collapse regimes favor gradient- and manifold-based scores. Building on these insights, we propose two contributions: a simple PCA-based projection-filtering procedure that improves detector performance, and an approach that uses only the NC measurements of a trained classifier to predict its competitive out-of-distribution detector shortlist, without OOD data for that classifier and without knowledge of the shift.

Machine Learning.title: DynSurvX: Time-Resolved Explanations for Dynamic Survival Predictions
Machine Learning.summary: Recent survival models integrating longitudinal data achieve strong predictive performance, but their predictions are often difficult to interpret, limiting their clinical use. We propose DynSurvX, a model-agnostic explainability framework for dynamic survival prediction with mixed static and longitudinal covariates. Based on Shapley values, DynSurvX introduces a hierarchical two-phase strategy that first identifies influential longitudinal features and then adaptively refines their temporal importance, enabling fine-grained explanations while reducing computational cost. The framework provides time-resolved explanations that evolve as new patient data become available. Experiments on simulated and two clinical datasets show varying agreement with theoretical importance across prediction models, with closer agreement for better-performing models, alongside clinically interpretable insights in real-world settings. It remains robust across prediction settings and reduces computation time by 41--80\% relative to the temporal explanation baseline, making dynamic explanations practical.

Machine Learning.title: When Do Histology Foundation Models Need Geometric Test-Time Augmentation?
Machine Learning.summary: Test-time augmentation (TTA) aggregates model predictions across multiple transformed views of an input during inference. Because histology images lack a canonical orientation, $D_4$ TTA---pooling across the 8 rotations and reflections of a square---is a standard default in computational pathology. However, the rise of self-supervised histology foundation models (FMs) with inherent rotational invariance calls its continued utility into question. We benchmark 9 histology FMs and 6 general-purpose models across four patch-level and two whole-slide image (WSI) datasets. We find that $D_4$ TTA remains a reliable post hoc improvement, but benefits diminish from $+1.98$ percentage points (pp) for general-purpose backbones to $+0.50$ pp for histology FMs on TCGA-UT, and shrink further for the largest models. To eliminate computational overhead, our experiments demonstrate that entropy routing---applying TTA selectively to uncertain predictions---recovers most of the gain while augmenting only ${\sim}13\%$ of samples. Finally, we show that patch-level TTA improvements do not transfer to slide-level multiple instance learning (MIL). Code: https://github.com/lars-chen/histology-tta

Machine Learning.title: Severe but Harmless: Stress-Testing Shift Severity for Frozen Time-Series Forecasters
Machine Learning.summary: Zero-shot time-series foundation models (TSFMs) have become attractive alternatives to task-specific models because they handle diverse downstream tasks, including anomaly detection and forecasting, without per-series training. However, time-series data undergo distribution shifts, and the dissimilarity between two regimes is commonly scored with statistical measures such as Wasserstein-1, where a higher score is read as a more severe shift. In systematic experiments using three established severity measures on nine regime shifts from three standard traffic datasets, we show that these measures do not reliably predict degradation for instance-normalized TSFMs. The regimes rated most severe are not the regimes that degrade the models most, and degradation reaches 29% in the lowest-scoring regime. In most cases, the audit shows no positive relationship between measured severity and model degradation. We provide an equivariance-based stress-testing analysis that explains why severity readings can become decoupled from model degradation.
Machine Learning.comment: 10 pages, 6 figures, 5 tables. Accepted at IEEE BigData 2026

Machine Learning.title: Reading or Remembering? Measuring Temporal Contamination in Language Models
Machine Learning.summary: Language models are now used to read central-bank text for economic forecasting, but most were trained on text written after the documents they read. A model reading a 2021 FOMC statement may already know that inflation rose in 2022, so part of its apparent skill can be memory of the outcome, a temporal form of test-set contamination. We measure this memory on FOMC statements and minutes from 2000 to 2026 by comparing modern open models with chronologically consistent models, which are trained only on text from before a fixed date. Asked about past GDP outcomes given only a date, models that cannot know the answer still reach an AUC of up to 0.64 from priors on dates and eras, so chance is the wrong baseline. Against these memory-free models on the same questions, most modern models recall which years had strong growth. Membership-inference scores sort documents by era and document type rather than by whether a model saw them, as exact counts in an open pretraining corpus show. In real-time nowcasts, every lookahead premium we estimate on US GDP is smaller than the forecast comparison can detect at macroeconomic sample sizes, and none on GDP or inflation survives correction for multiple testing. Lookahead audits should therefore measure memory directly against memory-free models on the same items.

Machine Learning.title: Benchmarking memory and nonlinear processing capacity of quantum recurrent neural networks for time series prediction
Machine Learning.summary: Quantum machine learning has emerged as a promising approach to time series prediction. While quantum reservoir computing has been widely explored for this setting, variational quantum models tailored to sequential data remain comparatively understudied, largely because they are difficult to train. In this work, we present a rigorous benchmark of variational quantum recurrent neural networks (QRNNs) on time series prediction tasks, focusing on two key capabilities: memory and nonlinear processing. We introduce a task-driven methodology that quantifies model capacity, enabling an intuitive and fair comparison across architectures, including classical recurrent baselines. We evaluate the proposed framework on two generic benchmark tasks and on a synthetic dataset describing a chaotic system. Overall, the quantum models achieve performance comparable to their classical counterparts, but classical models scale better with the memory size within the range studied. Notably, one QRNN variant shows higher average capacity on the task designed to jointly probe memory and nonlinear capacity. Moreover, our results show that quantum models offer better capacity when we are able to find a good parameter initialization. However, the increasing sensitivity to initialization leads to a lower probability of finding good solutions as the model size increases. These results provide a principled starting point for designing richer quantum recurrent architectures and for assessing where they may offer practical benefits.

Machine Learning.title: ONAM: Fitting Orthogonal Neural Additive Models for Post-Hoc Interpretability of Black-Box Predictions
Machine Learning.summary: Modern machine learning models, such as artificial neural networks, achieve high predictive performance through increasingly complex black-box architectures, limiting their use in settings where transparency, interpretability, and fairness are required. Here we present the R package ONAM, which provides a novel and practical implementation of functional decomposition, a technique to facilitate the interpretability of black-box models through structured effect representations. ONAM implements an algorithmic framework for the post-hoc decomposition of predictions into components associated with different input features. The package is designed for usability and efficiency, including functionalities for visualization as well as quantitative measures to assess interpretability. As a model-agnostic method, it can be applied to a wide range of prediction models. We describe the mathematical foundations, algorithmic design, and software architecture of ONAM. A central result of the proposed methodology is that the resulting decomposition satisfies the condition of hierarchical orthogonality, thereby guaranteeing that all components are identifiable and uniquely defined.

Machine Learning.title: The cost of enforcing long-run coverage: a phase transition in online conformal prediction
Machine Learning.summary:
Consider an online prediction setting, where at each time, we are given a new feature vector and asked to provide a prediction interval or prediction set that will likely contain the corresponding response. In this setting, if the data points are i.i.d. (or more generally, exchangeable), conformal prediction provides a mechanism for building valid prediction sets around the output of any trained model, offering coverage probability $\geq 1-α$ at each time $t$. In practice, however, issues such as distribution drift, changepoints, or other challenges may cause violations of the i.i.d. assumption. In this adversarial setting, online conformal prediction methods can still offer guarantees on long-run empirical coverage. However, there is a trade-off between these two types of goals: enforcing tight constraints on long-run empirical coverage to protect against the adversarial setting can lead to unstable oscillations in the instantaneous training-conditional coverage in the i.i.d. setting.
  In this work, we seek best-of-both-worlds algorithms that aim to minimize cumulative error in instantaneous training-conditional coverage when in the i.i.d. setting, while also offering long-run empirical coverage guarantees in the adversarial setting. Specifically, consider a condition that requires long-run empirical coverage to deviate from the target level $1-α$ by at most $\mathcal{O}(T^{-β})$, for some $β\in[0,1]$. We prove that this family of conditions can be described with a phase transition. For $β\in[0,\frac{1}{2}]$, it is possible to construct algorithms satisfying such a constraint in the adversarial setting, while offering the same instantaneous coverage performance as split conformal prediction if the data is in fact i.i.d. On the other hand, for $β\in(\frac{1}{2},1]$, this type of condition comes at a cost, and does not achieve best-of-both-worlds behavior.

Machine Learning.title: SciResearch-Eval: Evaluating Scientific Judgment in Autonomous Experimental Agents
Machine Learning.summary: We introduce SciResearch-Eval, an interactive benchmark of scientific judgment built on a standard laboratory problem: measuring a material's thermal properties by heating it and fitting a heat-conduction simulator. An agent designs its own experiments, uses a supplied simulator that may be under-resolved or physically wrong, and reports each property with a 95% interval. To our knowledge it is the first benchmark to combine agent-designed experiments, a deliberately flawed simulator, and proper scoring of calibrated intervals against exact ground truth. On a held-out split (93 tasks, 9 models, 2,511 episodes), models handle procedural traps. When the simulator is missing physics, most report wrong values while stating they are 95% sure: their ranges contain the truth in 20-62% of cases, against 94% for GPT-6 Astra and 99% for Claude Fable 5.2. At default effort the failing Claude 5.5 models rarely diagnose the missing physics (Opus in 35% of episodes, against 66% for Astra), and even when they do, their ranges often miss; Astra and Fable design experiments in which the flawed simulator is accurate, such as gentle heating, which keeps Astra calibrated even when it does not name the cause. Asking for wider intervals does not help; stating the strategy improves interval scores 1.6-2.5-fold, replicated on a pre-registered fresh split, but coverage barely moves. A pre-registered effort ablation shows that the correction is latent in the Claude 5.5 models: at maximum effort Opus improves more than tenfold and is no longer detectably behind Astra at default, but only with 13-31 times more reasoning; older and open-weight models gain nothing. Fable 5.2 is the most accurate model at default effort (interval score 1.9 times better than Astra's) but writes 6 times as many tokens, and at Astra's token count it falls short. We release the environment, graders and harness.

Machine Learning.title: Seen but Unsaid: Locating and Repairing Cross-Image Comparison in Vision-Language Models
Machine Learning.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) often fail to match a point or an object across two images, even when the answer can be decoded from their own hidden states. We trace this failure from the visual tokens to the answer letter, in Qwen3-VL (2B-32B), InternVL3.5-8B, and Gemma-3-12B, on synthetic shape matching, same-instance point correspondence (HPatches), and semantic correspondence (SPair-71k), and find two distinct failure points, a small set of attention heads that carries the comparison, and a repair that touches 0.02% of the parameters. Two failure points: exact copies are compared but not read out. An answer-position probe exceeds the calibrated output by 15 to 25 points in every family, for nameable and unnameable shapes alike, and steering along the probe's direction moves no more answers than random directions. Semantic correspondences are present in the visual tokens but never reach the answer. One pathway: redistributing the cross-image attention of 16-32 heads, with its mass preserved, removes 17-22 points of synthetic and 15-32 points of HPatches accuracy, against at most 7 for random or attention-matched heads. A lever that training finds on its own: training only these heads' query and key projections raises SPair-71k accuracy by 28.3 points (Qwen3-VL-8B) and 25.1 points (InternVL3.5-8B), beats both layer-matched and attention-matched heads, and transfers to HPatches and BLINK. An unconstrained all-layer adapter routes 21-51% of its gain through the attention of the same heads, against at most 7% for random heads, and does so by changing what they read (83-86% of the effect) rather than their weights. Every decision rule was frozen before its run, and every reported number is recomputed by independent verification scripts.

Machine Learning.title: Optimistic Verifiers Get Hacked: Reward Hacking Under an Exact Process Oracle
Machine Learning.summary: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards inherits whatever its verifier gets wrong. Outside mathematics and code the verifier is a proxy, a rubric, a learned judge or a hand-written checker, and its distance from the true objective is never measured, so a rising reward cannot be told apart from a hack. We build a setting where the true reward is exactly computable at the process level: executable authorization policies over 124,416 contexts admit an oracle that lists every minimal sufficient reason for every decision. We compile these policies into exact process rewards, degrade the verifier along seven realistic axes (outcome-only, sufficiency, recall-only, extraction noise, coarse taxonomy, stale policy, LLM judge), and train against each while the exact verifier scores every rollout. Four phenotypes appear. Optimistic verifiers are hacked by padding: the sufficiency proxy ends at 0.940 while true faithfulness falls from 0.731 to 0.667 on 96 held-out episodes. Outcome-only verifiers saturate and stop teaching, noise dilutes, and ranking-preserving gaps do no harm. A model-free audit of the verifier, its selection error and gap sign, together with a short saturation pilot, anticipates which phenotype a run will produce. Across nine configurations spanning two frameworks, two model vendors, two adapter sizes, three precisions, two initialisations and two seeds, the phenotypes recur, sufficiency damage is positive in all 10 replication cells and beyond two standard errors in 7, and optimistic gaps remain the steeper branch. The damage magnitude does not replicate, and five pre-registered attempts to explain it are reported as they fell. We release the testbed, the training instrumentation, and 14 real public policies (Cedar, OPA, Gatekeeper) ported to executable oracles.
Machine Learning.comment: 30 pages. A shorter version, "The Verifier Gap", appears at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Meta-Agents (non-archival)

Machine Learning.title: Procedure without Judgment: What Small Language Models Learn under an Exact Verifier
Machine Learning.summary: When an authorization policy blocks an agent's tool call, the audit log should name the facts that forced the decision and nothing more. For an executable policy over an enumerable context space this minimal sufficient reason can be computed exactly, so an explanation is scored against ground truth rather than a proxy for it. We use that exactness to ask what a model can learn from a verifier that has no error in it. The explainer sees one request and one decision, never the policy, and has thirty turns in which it may call the policy on altered requests and ask whether a candidate set of facts is sufficient. Frontier models find the exact reason about half the time with the tools alone, and one sentence telling them to shrink the answer lifts Haiku 4.5 from 58% to 75%. A 4B model fine-tuned on 2000 traces of the deletion algorithm reaches 92% on the policy it was trained on. Teacher kind is what moves this: at matched data size the algorithm-taught student leads the frontier-taught one in all three training seeds, and the two arms never overlap. What the student learns is a fixed schedule of sufficiency checks, and the schedule does not travel. On three public policies it never saw, its answers stay sufficient (94%) and stop being minimal (48%), while Haiku under the same sentence is exact on all 47 episodes. Reinforcement learning from the exact reward leaves held-out accuracy where it was and inverts the strategy, from probing the policy to spending the entire budget on sufficiency checks. The oracle made the effect of training legible, but it did not make training better.

Machine Learning.title: Toward LLM-Supported Automated Assessment of Critical Thinking Subskills
Machine Learning.summary: As the world becomes increasingly saturated with AI-generated content, disinformation, and algorithmic persuasion, critical thinking - the capacity to evaluate evidence, detect unreliable claims, and exercise independent judgment - is becoming a defining human skill. Developing critical thinking skills through timely assessment and feedback is crucial; however, there has not been extensive work in educational data mining on defining, measuring, and supporting critical thinking. In this paper, we investigate the feasibility of measuring "subskills" that underlie critical thinking. We ground our work in an authentic task where students operationalize critical thinking by writing argumentative essays. We developed a coding rubric based on an established skills progression and completed human coding for a corpus of student essays. We then evaluated three distinct approaches to automated scoring: zero-shot prompting, few-shot prompting, and supervised fine-tuning, implemented across three large language models (GPT-5, Llama 3.1 8B, and ModernBERT). Fine-tuning Llama 3.1 8B achieved the best results and demonstrated particular strength on subskills with highly separable proficiency levels with balanced labels across levels, while lower performance was observed for subskills that required detection of subtle distinctions between proficiency levels or imbalanced labels. Our exploratory work represents an initial step toward scalable assessment of critical thinking skills across authentic educational contexts. Future research should continue to combine automated critical thinking assessment with human validation to more accurately detect and measure dynamic, higher-order thinking skills.
Machine Learning.comment: Published in EDM 2026: Educational Data Mining Conference

Machine Learning.title: Algorithm Distillation for Safe In-Context Reinforcement Learning
Machine Learning.summary: Safe in-context reinforcement learning (Safe ICRL) asks a policy with fixed parameters to improve on an unseen constrained task from its interaction history while aiming to keep its cost within a budget. Prior work studied Safe ICRL on five benchmarks in three families: a grid world with a hidden goal and obstacles (DarkRoom), continuous navigation where goals and hazards stay invisible until reached (PointGoal, CarGoal), and locomotion with a hidden velocity limit (HalfCheetah, Ant). Safe Algorithm Distillation (Safe AD), trained on the learning histories of a safe RL algorithm, has shown adaptation failures in prior evaluations.
